name: Dana Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and isn't linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tuesdays and Thursdays I teach violin at the Eastside Music Hub, a council-funded music school in an old library. It's mostly kids aged eight to twelve, half-size violins, a lot of squeaking and a lot of rosin dust. At weekends I play second violin in the Linden Quartet, a string quartet that does weddings and the odd funeral. I'm still the weakest player of the four, honestly, and Mira who leads it tells me so, kindly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Which part of that week do you love, and which part drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a kid plays a whole tune without stopping and looks up shocked. What drains me is the admin, chasing parents for fees, writing lesson notes, answering wedding enquiries at midnight. I live with my flatmate Jo in a two-bed above a bakery, and I've got about three months of costs saved. I use a chatbot sometimes to tidy up emails to brides, but that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank goodness, now can we talk about arts funding instead. The real story for music teachers was never robots, it's councils cutting budgets. I'd probably post the Hub's fundraising page again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the Hub's funding is already shaky. The council cut two posts last spring and my hours could go next year whatever AI does. So a quiet AI world doesn't fix my problem; it just takes away the excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep the quartet bookings coming in. I'd use the chatbot a bit more for the email side, since it saves me an hour a week. And I'd start a couple of private pupils at home so I'm not fully tied to the Hub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other options, I suppose. But there's still that letter from the council in the back of my mind. I'd sleep fine, just not deeply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did that council letter actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It said the Hub's grant is under review for next year, which everyone knows means a cut. If the council cuts the Eastside Music Hub, forty kids lose their only violin lessons and I lose two days' pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many private pupils would you need to replace those two days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eight, at an hour each a week. I've got two right now. Getting to eight without a car means pupils coming to my flat, and Jo is very patient but not that patient.

say: I'd say the real threat to music teaching is **council cuts**, not AI.
I'd share the **Hub's fundraising** page again online.
think: My **two teaching days** could go next year because the grant is under review.
A quiet AI world just removes the **excuse**, not the funding problem.
do: Keep **teaching** at the Hub and taking quartet bookings.
Use the **chatbot** more for wedding emails to save an hour a week.
Build up to **eight private pupils** at home.
feel: Fairly **calm**, but the **council letter** keeps her from sleeping deeply.
S0.quote: If the council cuts the Eastside Music Hub, forty kids lose their only violin lessons and I lose two days' pay.
fieldNote: Her biggest pressure is **public funding**, which exists with or without AI.
She already uses AI lightly for **admin**, without fuss.
Space at home limits her **private teaching** plan.

steps.text: Keep teaching violin at the Eastside Music Hub on Tuesdays and Thursdays
Use the chatbot to draft replies to wedding enquiries
Take on six more private violin pupils at home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can write a lesson plan but it can't hold a ten-year-old's bow arm straight. That's the line I'd use. I'd also say the companies should pay into arts education if they're using all our music.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the quartet worries me more than the teaching. Couples already ask for a playlist instead of us to save money, and AI will make a perfect string version of any pop song for free. The teaching is hands-on and in a room, so I think that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift my week towards teaching, maybe ask the Hub for a third day if the funding holds. I'd learn the AI tools that help with practice, like the apps that listen to a kid play and mark the wrong notes. And I'd join the teachers' section of the musicians' union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but not frightened. I can see where I'd stand. It's the wedding money that would thin out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your income comes from weddings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third, more in summer. A good June is six weddings at a hundred and twenty each. A bride can already get a string version of a favourite pop song from an app, so the Linden Quartet has to be worth more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the quartet would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira, who leads it, because the quartet is basically her business and she's put everything into it. Mira would fight to keep it going long after it stopped paying. I'd help where I could, but I wouldn't hang my rent on it.

say: I'd say AI can't hold a **ten-year-old's bow arm** straight.
I'd argue AI firms should **pay into** arts education.
think: **Wedding bookings** thin out because AI makes free string versions of pop songs.
In-person **teaching** is hands-on and should last.
do: Ask the Hub for a **third teaching day** if the funding holds.
Learn **practice apps** that mark pupils' wrong notes.
feel: **Uneasy** about wedding money, but steady because teaching feels **solid**.
S1.quote: A bride can already get a string version of a favourite pop song from an app, so the Linden Quartet has to be worth more than that.
fieldNote: She reads her job as two parts: **teaching** survives, **weddings** shrink.
She'd adopt AI tools that are **proven** for practice, fitting her steady style.
Concern for **Mira**, the quartet leader, showed real loyalty.

steps.text: Ask the Eastside Music Hub for a third teaching day
Try a practice app that marks pupils' wrong notes
Join the musicians' union teachers' section

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a public plan, fast, with money for people who lose work. And I'd say children still need real teachers, so fund schools and music hubs properly. I'd be at the marches, probably with my violin case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, AGI in two years makes the admin and the weddings disappear first. Then robots arrive around 2031, though I don't think parents will hand their kids to a robot violin teacher. But if parents are losing their jobs, nobody pays for lessons, and that's what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my spending, cancel the new bow I've been saving for, and keep the three months intact. I'd ask the Hub about a contract instead of hourly pay. I'd start looking at teaching jobs in schools, which might need a qualification I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a knot in my stomach. Not because I'll be replaced by a machine tomorrow, but because the people paying me might be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the risk is less the robots and more the parents' wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly. Violin lessons are the first thing a family cuts when money's tight. A robot won't take my violin pupils, but a parent losing an office job will cancel lessons the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go back to study for that teaching qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, but it's a year full-time and I'd burn through my savings. Maybe part-time over two years if the Hub gave me steady days. I'd ask Jo if we could cut the rent by moving somewhere smaller.

say: I'd call for a **public plan** with money for people who lose work.
I'd march for proper **funding** of schools and music hubs.
think: Weddings and admin go first, then **parents' wages** drop and lessons get cancelled.
Robots arriving around **2031** won't replace in-person teaching, but customers can't pay.
do: Cancel the **new bow** and keep three months saved.
Ask the Hub for a **contract** instead of hourly pay.
feel: A **knot** in her stomach about who will still **afford lessons**.
S2.quote: A robot won't take my violin pupils, but a parent losing an office job will cancel lessons the same week.
fieldNote: She sees risk through her **customers' jobs**, not her own replaceability.
Her savings make **full-time study** feel too costly.
Moving to a **smaller flat** with Jo came up as a real option.

steps.text: Cancel the new bow purchase and protect three months' savings
Ask the Hub for a fixed contract instead of hourly pay
Apply for a part-time music teaching qualification
Join marches calling for public funding of music hubs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd say there's no excuse for councils to keep cutting arts. I'd be pushing for music to stay in every school. I'd be more organised about it, writing to councillors rather than just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the weddings fade over three or four years and the teaching holds, if families have money. Five years is enough to get the qualification, which changes things. I'd be a proper school music teacher by the time AGI lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the part-time teaching course next autumn and keep the Hub days going. I'd drop weddings slowly, keeping the summer ones. I'd save a bit more each month for the course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan to hold onto. It's less like a knot and more like homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the kids at the Hub about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't scare them. I'd tell them that playing an instrument trains your patience and your ears, and no machine can do your practice for you. Nobody learns the violin to beat a computer at it; you learn the violin to hear what you couldn't hear before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss the quartet if you dropped it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Terribly. Saturday afternoons with Mira and the others are when I feel most like a musician. I'd keep one or two a month just for that, even if they barely pay.

say: I'd say councils have **no excuse** to cut arts with five years' warning.
I'd write to **councillors** to keep music in every school.
think: Weddings fade over **three or four years** while teaching holds.
Five years is enough time to get a **teaching qualification**.
do: Start a **part-time teaching course** next autumn.
Save extra each month for **course fees**.
feel: Still **anxious**, but it feels more like **homework** than a knot.
S3.quote: Nobody learns the violin to beat a computer at it; you learn the violin to hear what you couldn't hear before.
fieldNote: The extra years let her turn worry into a **qualification plan**.
She frames music as **training the ear**, not competing with machines.
The **quartet** matters to her identity more than her income.

steps.text: Start a part-time school music teaching course next autumn
Save extra each month towards course fees
Write to local councillors about keeping music in schools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to rebuild arts education properly, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. I'd also say this is when unions should be negotiating, not waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels like a career, honestly. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI lands, qualified and settled in a school, I hope. The worry is the same end point, but it's far enough off that I'd be in a stronger place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the qualification over two or three years, keep a couple of weddings, and keep my private pupils. I'd learn the AI teaching tools properly once schools adopt them. I'd keep my savings steady rather than cutting back hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. There's a small worry about the end point, but it's not running my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with a decade that you wouldn't with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd maybe think about having a family, which I haven't let myself think about with my income. With ten years to plan, I could finally imagine being a violin teacher with a salary, a pension and a kid of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Jo, the flatmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo would probably be long gone by then, married, I'd guess. My flatmate Jo once told me I'm the only person who'd rather tune a stranger's child's violin than go to the pub. That's still true.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **rebuild arts education** properly.
I'd push **unions** to negotiate now instead of waiting.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven**, qualified and settled in a school when AGI lands.
The **end point** is the same, but I'd face it stronger.
do: Finish a **teaching qualification** over two or three years.
Keep a few **weddings** and private pupils.
Learn school **AI teaching tools** once schools adopt them.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a small worry about the **end point**.
S4.quote: With ten years to plan, I could finally imagine being a violin teacher with a salary, a pension and a kid of my own.
fieldNote: A decade lets her picture a **salary and pension**, which she hadn't allowed before.
**Family plans** only appear in the longest scenario.
She'd learn AI tools **after schools** adopt them, true to her steady approach.

steps.text: Finish a school music teaching qualification within three years
Learn the AI teaching tools her school adopts
Keep two private pupils and a few summer weddings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's not my teaching that goes but the parents' wages, and then the lessons go with them. What would help is public money for music in schools so lessons don't depend on what parents can afford, and support for people who lose their jobs so families aren't cutting everything at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what music is for. Everyone talks about jobs, but for those forty kids at the Hub, the violin is the one hour a week nobody's shouting at them. That matters whatever happens with AI.

headlineQuote: My flatmate Jo once told me I'm the only person who'd rather tune a stranger's child's violin than go to the pub.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old violin teacher** at a council-funded music school who plays weddings in a quartet.
She has about **three months saved**, shares a flat with Jo and sees council cuts as her main threat.
She's **progressive** and pushes for public arts funding, using AI lightly for admin.
She expects **weddings to fade** while hands-on teaching lasts, if parents can still pay.
Longer warning times turn her worry into a **teaching qualification** plan and even family hopes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because parents losing jobs would cancel **lessons** fast.
whatWouldHelp: **Public funding** for music in schools so lessons don't depend on parents' money.
**Support for families** who lose work so they don't cut everything at once.
